extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate or beginning graduate students studying real analysis (sequences & series)
extracted.subtask_description: Textbook section giving definitions, propositions, and proof techniques for determining convergence and limits of real sequences (including roots, absolute values, ratio test, limsup/liminf, Bolzano–Weierstrass, and Cauchy sequences). Designed to guide writing rigorous proofs and computations about sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taking limits through roots and continuous operations
rubrics_metrics.description: If (x_n)_{n=1}^∞ is a convergent sequence and x_n ≥ 0 for all n with lim_{n→∞} x_n = x, then lim_{n→∞} √x_n = √x. A similar proof works for the k-th root: lim_{n→∞} x_n^{1/k} = x^{1/k}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof splits cases x = 0 and x > 0: for x = 0 use ε^2 and show √x_n < ε eventually; for x > 0 rationalize difference or use algebraic manipulations to bound |√x_n - √x| by |x_n - x|/√x (or similar). Ensure nonnegativity before taking real roots. The converse (taking limits under root implying original limits) is not generally true (see exercises).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit through absolute value
rubrics_metrics.description: If (x_n) is a convergent sequence with limit x, then lim_{n→∞} |x_n| = |x|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the reverse triangle inequality | |x_n| - |x| | ≤ |x_n - x| to show |x_n| can be made arbitrarily close to |x|. Note the converse is not true in general (see Exercise 2.1.7 part b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful algebraic manipulation before taking limits
rubrics_metrics.description: You must ensure sequences involved converge before applying limit laws or separating terms; naive algebraic splitting can produce nonsense when individual pieces do not converge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: rewriting expressions with a common denominator may be necessary; do not take limits termwise if the individual terms (or their limits) do not exist. Read equalities right-to-left when using existence of limits of the RHS to justify existence on the LHS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for recursively defined sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: To analyze a sequence defined recursively (x_{n+1} given in terms of previous x_n,...), first show the sequence is well-defined (e.g., never dividing by zero), then show convergence by establishing monotonicity and boundedness, and only then attempt to find the limit by taking limits in the recursion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical steps: (1) Verify base case (e.g., x_1 > 0). (2) Use induction to prove properties such as positivity. (3) Prove monotone (increasing/decreasing) and bounded, hence convergent. (4) Let limit be x and substitute into the recursion to solve for x (be careful about extraneous roots and dependence on initial value). Example: Newton's method iteration for √r—show positivity, monotone behavior, then limit satisfies quadratic equation giving √r (sign depending on x_1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison via vanishing error sequences (Proposition 2.2.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: If there exists a convergent sequence (a_n) with lim_{n→∞} a_n = 0 and |x_n - x| ≤ a_n for all n, then (x_n) converges and lim_{n→∞} x_n = x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the standard ε-definition: given ε>0 pick M with a_n<ε for n≥M, then |x_n - x| ≤ a_n < ε. This reduces checking convergence to checking a vanishing bound sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior of geometric sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: For c>0: if c<1 then c^n → 0 as n→∞; if c>1 then (c^n)_{n=1}^∞ is unbounded (hence diverges).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove monotonicity and boundedness when c<1 (use induction to show decreasing and bounded below) to deduce convergence; for c>1 use comparison to show terms exceed any given bound for sufficiently large n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratio test for sequences (Lemma 2.2.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let x_n ≠ 0 for all n and suppose L = lim_{n→∞} |x_{n+1}/x_n| exists. If L < 1 then x_n → 0. If L > 1 then (x_n) is unbounded (hence diverges). If L = 1 the test is inconclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: pick r with L < r < 1 to dominate eventual ratios and compare to a geometric sequence r^{n}. For L > 1 pick r with 1 < r < L to show ratio eventually exceeds r and hence grows like r^{n}, so unbounded. The lemma can be strengthened to require the ratio bound only eventually (see exercises).

rubrics_metrics.name: Squeeze (sandwich) lemma for sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: If a_n ≤ x_n ≤ b_n for all sufficiently large n and lim_{n→∞} a_n = lim_{n→∞} b_n = L, then lim_{n→∞} x_n = L.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard ε-argument: control difference via the bounds; used repeatedly (e.g., for limits that are tails of sequences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotone bounded sequence convergence (used repeatedly)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence that is monotone (increasing or decreasing) and bounded converges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use induction to establish monotonicity and check bounds (e.g., positivity gives lower bound); then apply monotone convergence theorem to deduce existence of a limit (used for geometric sequences, recursively defined sequences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and computation of lim sup and lim inf
rubrics_metrics.description: For a bounded sequence (x_n) define a_n = sup_{k≥n} x_k and b_n = inf_{k≥n} x_k. Then (a_n) is decreasing, (b_n) is increasing, and limsup_{n→∞} x_n = lim_{n→∞} a_n, liminf_{n→∞} x_n = lim_{n→∞} b_n. For bounded sequences these limits always exist and liminf ≤ limsup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute limsup/liminf by analyzing sup/inf of tails. The definitions extend to unbounded sequences by allowing ±∞. Use these quantities to characterize convergence: sequence converges iff limsup = liminf.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subsequential limits and constructing subsequences achieving limsup/liminf (Theorem 2.3.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If (x_n) is bounded, there exists a subsequence converging to limsup_{n→∞} x_n and another subsequence converging to liminf_{n→∞} x_n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: pick indices n_k where x_{n_k} is within 1/k of the tail supremum a_{n_k}; an inductive selection yields a subsequence converging to the limsup. Similar construction for liminf. This shows limsup is the largest subsequential limit and liminf the smallest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Every bounded sequence of real numbers has a convergent subsequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can be proved by Theorem 2.3.4 (use subsequence approaching limsup) or by nested-interval-style construction: repeatedly choose subintervals that contain infinitely many terms and cut their length in half to produce monotone sequences of endpoints whose limit is the subsequential limit. Useful as a tool to extract convergent subsequences from bounded sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowing infinite limits and extended limsup/liminf
rubrics_metrics.description: Extend definitions so lim_{n→∞} x_n = +∞ means terms eventually exceed any K; similarly for −∞. Extended limsup and liminf can be defined in the extended real line to handle unbounded sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For monotone unbounded sequences: increasing unbounded ⇒ limit +∞; decreasing unbounded ⇒ limit −∞. When working with limsup/liminf allow ±∞ values when sequences are unbounded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy sequence test and basic properties
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence (x_n) is Cauchy if for every ε>0 there exists M such that for all n,k ≥ M we have |x_n - x_k| < ε. Cauchy sequences have the property that terms eventually cluster together and need not reference a limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Cauchy criterion to test convergence when the limit is unknown; in ℝ completeness implies Cauchy ⇔ convergent (the section begins with definition and proves Cauchy ⇒ bounded). Provide examples: (1/n) is Cauchy; the sequence (−1)^n is not Cauchy. Basic proof that every Cauchy sequence is bounded uses reverse triangle inequality and a finite initial segment to bound all terms.
